title: AM versus NP
formal:
Does \(\mathrm{AM}=\mathrm{NP}\)? Equivalently, does every language having an Arthur–Merlin protocol admit polynomial-length certificates checked deterministically in polynomial time?

For a language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\), an Arthur–Merlin protocol is specified by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) and polynomially bounded lengths \(p(n),q(n)\). Arthur draws a uniform public string \(r\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\); after seeing \(x\) and \(r\), Merlin may choose a reply \(y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}\). With \(n=|x|\), require
\[x\in L\Longrightarrow\Pr_r[\exists y:\ V(x,r,y)=1]\ge\tfrac23,\]
\[x\notin L\Longrightarrow\Pr_r[\exists y:\ V(x,r,y)=1]\le\tfrac13.\]
Must there exist a deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(W\) and a polynomially bounded length \(s(n)\) such that, for every binary string \(x\),
\[x\in L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists z\in\{0,1\}^{s(|x|)}:\ W(x,z)=1?\]
The resulting verifier and its polynomial bounds may depend on \(L\), but must work uniformly at all input lengths.
why: This asks whether short randomized interaction gives more verification power than static certificates. It is a fundamental derandomization question beyond decision algorithms, with consequences for certifying graph nonisomorphism and with close links to nondeterministic circuit hardness.
status_note: Source-open in Vadhan’s 2012 monograph and explicitly retained as open in van Melkebeek–Mocelin Sdroievski, Computational Complexity 34, article 15 (23 October 2025), introduction. On 16 September 2026 this review checked the original definition and graph consequence, the exact hardness hypothesis of Miltersen–Vinodchandran Theorem 1.5, and the model and scope of the 2025 Theorems 1.6 and 1.12. The latter unconditional result is an average-case, infinitely-often simulation with advice in a stronger quantified model and does not place AM in NP. Bounded subsequent searches found no unconditional equality or separation for the stated ordinary-language target. The review checks theorem statements and applicability, not every technical proof in the 86-page journal article.

progress.text: Miltersen and Vinodchandran obtain AM equality with NP under exponential single-valued nondeterministic circuit hardness, improving earlier hardness assumptions.
Vadhan records the general derandomization question, its graph-nonisomorphism consequence and a precise conditional collapse.

Van Melkebeek and Mocelin Sdroievski establish further conditional hardness and refutation connections and an unconditional average-case simulation with weaker resource and uniformity guarantees; the full AM versus NP question remains open in that published source.

importance.reason: A major comparison between standard proof-system complexity classes, isolating the role of public randomness and interaction. It has a compelling concrete consequence for graph nonisomorphism and a substantial body of conditional and recent structural results.

sentences: Arthur–Merlin protocols let a prover choose a polynomial-length reply after seeing the verifier’s public random challenge.
The question asks whether every language with such a protocol also has ordinary NP certificates.
The verifier must be uniform and polynomial time, with completeness and soundness on every input.
Graph nonisomorphism would acquire static polynomially checkable certificates if the equality holds, but is not assumed complete for the whole question.
Known conditional derandomization and weaker recent simulations leave the unconditional class comparison open.

definitions:
Languages are subsets of the finite binary strings. Every input string is either a yes-instance in the language or a no-instance outside it; the target is an equality of ordinary language classes. There is no omitted promise domain. Input size \(n\) is the full bit length of \(x\), and the empty input is allowed.

Use classical uniform multitape Turing machines with finite descriptions. A polynomial time bound means \(C(n+1)^a\) steps for some fixed constants \(C\ge1\) and integer \(a\ge0\). In a verifier taking several strings, time is polynomial in their total encoded length; the stated polynomial message bounds make this polynomial in \(n\) on protocol inputs. The verifier terminates on every such tuple, including misleading messages. It has no advice depending on the input length, oracle or quantum operation. All communication consists of ordinary binary strings.

The functions \(p,q,s:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) are computable in polynomial time and bounded by fixed polynomials. They may be taken to be integer-coefficient polynomial bounds, with unused bits ignored. Messages have the indicated exact lengths. Permitting shorter messages with a length encoding and padding gives the same class. Malformed messages are rejected according to the chosen verifier; they cannot provide an extra form of communication or uncounted computation.

The protocol has two messages: Arthur’s random challenge followed by Merlin’s reply. Arthur samples \(p(n)\) independent fair bits, so each challenge has probability \(2^{-p(n)}\). All of these bits are public before Merlin replies. The verifier’s final computation \(V(x,r,y)\) is deterministic; there is no additional hidden random tape. A zero-length challenge or reply is permitted. The polynomial defining each length is fixed for the protocol, not chosen separately for individual inputs.

Merlin is computationally unbounded. He knows the entire input and challenge and may choose a different reply for every pair \((x,r)\). Thus the existential quantifier over \(y\) is inside the probability over \(r\). Completeness says that on each yes-instance an accepting reply exists for at least two thirds of the challenges. Soundness says that on each no-instance an accepting reply exists for at most one third of them, even with an unbounded dishonest prover. Randomizing Merlin’s reply cannot increase the set of challenges for which some accepting reply exists.

These two probability conditions define \(\mathrm{AM}\). They are per-input guarantees. Neither the inputs nor Merlin’s strategy are averaged over an external distribution. The soundness bound is information-theoretic: it is not limited to efficient cheating provers. The fixed gap between two thirds and one third is part of the chosen standard definition; ordinary amplification yields equivalent constant-gap conventions. Perfect completeness is not an added requirement of this card.

The class \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages with a verifier \(W\) and certificate length \(s\) satisfying the displayed exact equivalence. On yes-instances at least one certificate is accepted, and on no-instances every certificate is rejected. The verifier is deterministic and has no random challenge. The certificate itself need not be found in polynomial time. A proof of AM containment in NP must establish existence of these certificates and their efficient verification, not efficient deterministic decision or witness generation.

The inclusion \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{AM}\) is immediate by letting the AM verifier ignore its challenge. Thus equality asks for the converse inclusion. A positive answer must cover every AM language. A negative answer must exhibit, or prove the existence of, an AM language that has no polynomially bounded deterministic certificate system. Failure of one proposed verifier, one circuit family or one polynomial exponent does not establish such a separation.

The quantifier order is \(\forall L\in\mathrm{AM}\;\exists W\;\exists s\;\forall x\), with a fixed polynomial running-time bound for each \(W\). There is no common required exponent for all languages. Equality of language classes does not additionally require a computable compiler from protocol descriptions to NP verifiers, although a proved general transformation would suffice. A certificate system whose exponent changes with the individual input is not polynomially bounded in this sense.

The related class \(\mathrm{MA}\) reverses the message order: Merlin supplies a certificate before Arthur’s fresh random choices. Moving \(\exists y\) outside the probability changes the condition and must not be done here. Standard results identify AM with constant-round interactive proofs, but the explicit two-message public-coin definition above is the target model. Protocols with an input-dependent polynomial number of rounds are not the target.

A promise problem consists of disjoint sets \(Y,N\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\), with no correctness requirement outside \(Y\cup N\). The notation \(\mathrm{prAM}\) refers to the analogous promise-protocol class. A claim that every promise-AM problem has a separating NP language is stronger than the ordinary language inclusion asked here and is not assumed equivalent. This distinction matters for the neighboring targeted-generator question TCS-1135 and for several recent derandomization theorems.

Graph nonisomorphism is an example consequence, not a completeness reformulation. A finite simple undirected graph has no loops or parallel edges; two such graphs are isomorphic if some bijection between their vertex sets preserves adjacency. Graph nonisomorphism asks whether no such bijection exists, for explicitly encoded graph pairs. An NP certificate for nonisomorphism would be a polynomial-length binary witness of that negative assertion checked in polynomial time. Since graph nonisomorphism has an AM protocol, AM equality with NP would supply such certificates. Solving only that graph problem would not establish the full class equality without an additional proved completeness reduction.

For the conditional progress cited below, \(\mathrm{NE}=\bigcup_{c\ge1}\mathrm{NTIME}(2^{cn})\) and \(\mathrm{coNE}\) is its complement class. A single-valued nondeterministic Boolean circuit has ordinary input bits, auxiliary choice bits, and two outputs: a flag and a value bit. For every input some choice must set the flag to one, and every choice with flag one must give the correct value of the function. Choices with flag zero are ignored. Circuit size counts gates in a fixed fan-in-two AND/OR and unary NOT basis, together with auxiliary input bits. Circuits may vary nonuniformly with the input length. An exponential lower bound means that some \(\alpha>0\) requires size at least \(2^{\alpha n}\) for every sufficiently large length \(n\). This hardness hypothesis belongs to the cited conditional result and is not a premise of the question.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof that \(\mathrm{AM}\subseteq\mathrm{NP}\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that some language lies in \(\mathrm{AM}\setminus\mathrm{NP}\), with the specified verifier, message-order, uniformity and probability conventions. Equality must supply the existence of polynomial-length certificates and deterministic polynomial-time verification for every AM language on every input. It need not supply a deterministic decision algorithm or an efficient way to find the certificates. A separation must rule out every NP verifier and polynomial certificate bound for the chosen language. Conditional collapses, oracle results, simulations with advice, average-input correctness, larger time bounds and a certificate system only for graph nonisomorphism do not settle the unconditional class comparison. The default numerical approximation tolerance does not apply to this exact proposition.

source_formulation.text: Vadhan discusses removing randomness from Arthur–Merlin verification and identifies AM = NP as the general class comparison. Graph nonisomorphism in NP is given as a consequence. This card retains the full class equality and treats the graph problem as motivation, correcting the inherited page locator.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of §2.6 and §7.7.1; the class target and its example consequence are distinguished

context_blocks.text: An NP proof is one static certificate that a deterministic verifier can check. In an Arthur–Merlin protocol, the prover first sees a fresh public challenge and can tailor the proof to it. The question asks whether this additional use of randomness and interaction changes which languages have efficient proofs.

The placement of the existential reply inside the probability is the defining feature. Different challenges may need different valid replies. A deterministic certificate system must verify the same membership claim without asking for that random challenge, while retaining polynomial certificate length and verification time.

Graph nonisomorphism illustrates why this matters. A relabeling certifies that graphs are isomorphic, while certifying that no relabeling works is a different verification task. The known AM protocol for nonisomorphism gives an interactive justification; equality with NP would guarantee static, efficiently checkable certificates.

Miltersen and Vinodchandran show that an exponential lower bound against single-valued nondeterministic circuits for a language in the intersection of nondeterministic and co-nondeterministic exponential time implies AM equality with NP. The published theorem weakens earlier circuit-hardness hypotheses, but does not establish the required hardness premise.

The 2025 work of van Melkebeek and Mocelin Sdroievski develops conditional connections between Arthur–Merlin derandomization and uniform hardness or constructive refutation. Its main near-equivalences carefully distinguish ordinary protocols from promise protocols and account for advice. These are refinements of the conditions under which derandomization follows, not an unconditional collapse.

The same paper gives an unconditional weaker simulation in a different resource model: it uses a second-level quantified machine, subexponential time and a short advice string, and is guaranteed on most inputs at infinitely many lengths. Its theorem therefore leaves several requirements of ordinary NP verification unmet, including the time bound, lack of advice and correctness on all inputs.

A positive answer would eliminate random interaction as a source of additional polynomial-time proof power for this class. It would not make NP membership efficiently decidable. A negative answer would establish that some efficiently verifiable interactive claims inherently lack static polynomial-time certificates.
